{{Short description|Sum in algebraic number theory}}
{{distinguish|Triangular Number#Formula}}
In [[algebraic number theory]], a '''Gauss sum''' or '''Gaussian sum''' is a particular kind of finite [[Summation|sum]] of [[roots of unity]], typically

:<math>G(\chi) := G(\chi, \psi)= \sum \chi(r)\cdot \psi(r)</math>

where the sum is over elements {{mvar|r}} of some [[finite ring|finite]] [[commutative ring]] {{mvar|R}}, {{math|''ψ''}} is a [[group homomorphism]] of the [[group scheme|additive group]] {{math|''R''<sup>+</sup>}} into the [[unit circle]], and {{math|''χ''}} is a group homomorphism of the [[unit group]] {{math|''R''<sup>×</sup>}} into the unit circle, extended to non-unit {{mvar|r}}, where it takes the value&nbsp;0. Gauss sums are the analogues for finite fields of the [[Gamma function]].<ref>B. H. Gross and N. Koblitz. Gauss sums and the p-adic Γ-function. Ann. of Math. (2), 109(3):569–581,
1979.</ref><!---{{clarify|date=November 2015}}--->

Such sums are ubiquitous in [[number theory]]. They occur, for example, in the functional equations of [[Dirichlet L-function|Dirichlet {{mvar|L}}-function]]s, where for a [[Dirichlet character]] {{mvar|χ}} the equation relating {{math|''L''(''s'', ''χ'')}} and {{math|''L''(1&nbsp;−&nbsp;''s'', ''{{overline|χ}}''}}) (where {{mvar|{{overline|χ}}}} is the [[complex conjugate]] of {{mvar|χ}}) involves a factor{{clarify|date=August 2016}}

:<math>\frac{ G(\chi) }{ |G(\chi)| }. </math>

== History ==

The case originally considered by [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]] was the [[quadratic Gauss sum]], for {{mvar|R}} the [[residue field|field of residues]] [[modular arithmetic|modulo]] a [[prime number]] {{mvar|p}}, and {{mvar|χ}} the [[Legendre symbol]]. In this case Gauss proved that {{math|''G''(''χ'') {{=}} ''p''<sup>{{1/2}}</sup>}} or  {{math|''ip''<sup>{{1/2}}</sup>}} for {{mvar|p}} congruent to 1 or 3 modulo 4 respectively (the quadratic Gauss sum can also be evaluated by Fourier analysis as well as by [[contour integration]]).

An alternate form for this Gauss sum is
:<math>\sum e^{2 \pi i r^2/p}</math>.

Quadratic Gauss sums are closely connected with the theory of [[theta function]]s.

The general theory of Gauss sums was developed in the early 19th century, with the use of [[Jacobi sum]]s and their [[prime decomposition]] in [[cyclotomic field]]s. Gauss sums over a residue ring of integers {{math|mod ''N''}} are linear combinations of closely related sums called [[Gaussian period]]s.

The absolute value of Gauss sums is usually found as an application of [[Plancherel's theorem]] on finite groups. In the case where {{mvar|R}} is a field of {{mvar|p}} elements and {{mvar|χ}} is nontrivial, the absolute value is {{math|''p''<sup>{{1/2}}</sup>}}. The determination of the exact value of general Gauss sums, following the result of Gauss on the quadratic case, is a long-standing issue. For some cases see [[Kummer sum]].

==Properties of Gauss sums of Dirichlet characters==
The Gauss sum of a [[Dirichlet character]] modulo {{mvar|N}} is
:<math>G(\chi)=\sum_{a=1}^N\chi(a)e^{2\pi ia/N}.</math>
If {{mvar|χ}} is also [[primitive Dirichlet character|primitive]], then
:<math>|G(\chi)|=\sqrt{N},</math>
in particular, it is nonzero. More generally, if {{math|''N''<sub>0</sub>}} is the [[conductor of a Dirichlet character|conductor]] of {{mvar|χ}} and {{math|''χ''<sub>0</sub>}} is the primitive Dirichlet character modulo {{math|''N''<sub>0</sub>}} that induces {{mvar|χ}}, then the Gauss sum of {{mvar|χ}} is related to that of {{math|''χ''<sub>0</sub>}} by

:<math>G(\chi)=\mu\left(\frac{N}{N_0}\right)\chi_0\left(\frac{N}{N_0}\right)G\left(\chi_0\right)</math>

where {{mvar|μ}} is the [[Möbius function]]. Consequently, {{math|''G''(''χ'')}} is non-zero precisely when {{math|{{sfrac|''N''|''N''<sub>0</sub>}}}} is [[squarefree]] and [[relatively prime]] to {{math|''N''<sub>0</sub>}}.<ref>Theorem 9.10 in H. L. Montgomery, R. C. Vaughan, ''Multiplicative number theory. I. Classical theory'', Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics, '''97''', (2006).</ref>

Other relations between {{math|''G''(''χ'')}} and Gauss sums of other characters include

:<math>G(\overline{\chi})=\chi(-1)\overline{G(\chi)},</math>

where {{mvar|{{overline|χ}}}} is the complex conjugate Dirichlet character, and if {{math|''χ''′}} is a Dirichlet character modulo {{math|''N''′}} such that {{mvar|N}} and {{math|''N''′}} are relatively prime, then

:<math> G\left(\chi\chi^\prime\right) = \chi\left(N^\prime\right) \chi^\prime(N) G(\chi) G\left(\chi^\prime\right). </math>

The relation among {{math|''G''(''χχ''′)}}, {{math|''G''(''χ'')}}, and {{math|''G''(''χ''′)}} when {{mvar|χ}} and {{math|''χ''′}} are of the ''same'' modulus (and {{math|''χχ''′}} is primitive) is measured by the [[Jacobi sum]] {{math|''J''(''χ'', ''χ''′)}}. Specifically,
:<math>G\left(\chi\chi^\prime\right)=\frac{G(\chi)G\left(\chi^\prime\right)}{J\left(\chi,\chi^\prime\right)}.</math>

==Further properties==
*Gauss sums can be used to prove [[Proofs of quadratic reciprocity|quadratic reciprocity]], [[cubic reciprocity]], and [[quartic reciprocity]].
*Gauss sums can be used to calculate the number of solutions of polynomial equations over finite fields, and thus can be used to calculate certain zeta functions.
